## Claude_Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

An \KWD{extends} clause comes first, if any, and
\KWD{excludes},
\KWD{comprises},
and \KWD{where}
clauses come in any order.

Each of \KWD{extends}, \KWD{excludes}, and \KWD{comprises} clauses consists
of \KWD{extends}, \KWD{excludes}, and \KWD{comprises}
respectively followed by a set of trait references
separated by commas and enclosed in braces `\txt{\{}' and `\txt{\}}'.
If such a clause contains only one trait, the enclosing braces may be elided.
In an API (but not a component),
a \KWD{comprises} clause may include ``\EXP{\ldots}''.
A trait reference listed in the \KWD{comprises} clause is a declared
trait identifier (within the same component or an API imported by the
component).
\note{
Victor: Why is this property stated only for a comprises clause?
Doesn't it apply to extends and excludes clauses as well?
Also, do we really mean ``trait identifier'' above?  Where is that
term defined?  Does it include instantiations of parametric traits?}

A trait with an \KWD{extends} clause
\emph{explicitly extends} those traits listed in its \KWD{extends} clause.
\note{
Victor: It is possible for a trait to explicitly extend itself
 using hidden type variables.  In particular, the straightforward
 interpretation of covariant/contravariant declarations has this property.
 (But we could just rule this a special case, since it is special in other
 ways already.)
}
\revision{revival-where}{The revival rules on this note and on the
one below: a \KWD{where}-clause variable may not appear as a static
argument in an \KWD{extends} clause (\secref{where-clauses}),
so no trait extends itself through a hidden type variable
and explicit extension has no self cycles.}
In addition, every trait except \TYP{Any} and \TYP{Object}
implicitly extends the trait \TYP{Object}
if it does not do so explicitly.
We define the extension relation to be the transitive closure
of implicit and
explicit extension.
That is, trait \VAR{T} \emph{extends} trait \VAR{U}
if and only if \VAR{T} explicitly or implicitly
extends \VAR{U} or if there is some trait \VAR{S}
that \VAR{T} explicitly extends and that extends \VAR{U}.
The extension relation induced by a program is the smallest
relation satisfying these conditions.
This relation must form an acyclic hierarchy
rooted at trait \TYP{Object}.
\note{
Victor: Technically, there may be self cycles in explicit extension due to
 hidden type variables, as described above.}
If a trait \VAR{T} extends trait \VAR{U},
or if \VAR{T} and \VAR{U} are the same trait,
we say that \VAR{T} is a subtrait of \VAR{U}
and that \VAR{U} is a supertrait of \VAR{T}.

We say that trait \VAR{T} \emph{strictly extends} trait \VAR{U}
if and only if
(\emph{i}) \VAR{T} extends \VAR{U} and (\emph{ii}) \VAR{T} is not \VAR{U}.
We say that trait \VAR{T} \emph{immediately extends} trait \VAR{U}
\note{
Victor: I think we don't use ``immediately extends'' anywhere in the spec,
  only ``immediate supertype/subtype''.}
if and only if (\emph{i}) \VAR{T} strictly extends \VAR{U} and
(\emph{ii}) there is no trait \VAR{V}
such that \VAR{T} strictly extends \VAR{V}
and \VAR{V} strictly extends \VAR{U}.
We call \VAR{U} an \emph{immediate supertrait} of \VAR{T}
and \VAR{T} an \emph{immediate subtrait} of \VAR{U}.
\note{Victor: this belongs in the type chapter.}

A trait with an \KWD{excludes} clause excludes
every trait listed in its \KWD{excludes} clause.
If a trait \VAR{T} excludes a trait \VAR{U},
the two traits are mutually exclusive:
neither can extend the other, and no trait can extend them both.
As discussed in \secref{type-relations},
the exclusion relation is symmetric.
Thus, if \VAR{T} excludes \VAR{U}
then \VAR{U} excludes \VAR{T}
whether or not \VAR{T} is listed in an \KWD{excludes} clause
in the declaration of \VAR{U}.

If a trait declaration of \VAR{T} includes a \KWD{comprises} clause
then every type listed in its \KWD{comprises} clause extends \VAR{T},
and every value of type \VAR{T} is a value of one of the listed types.
A listed type may be an instantiation of a parameterized trait,
provided that every static variable that occurs in its static arguments
is a static parameter of \VAR{T}.
A trait or object that explicitly extends \VAR{T}
must be a subtype of a listed type,
unless it is a trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause of its own
each of whose listed types meets this requirement,
or a trait with static parameters
such that at least one trait or object extends it
and every trait or object that extends it
is a subtype of a listed type.
If \VAR{T} has static parameters,
these statements hold of each instantiation of \VAR{T},
with the static parameters of \VAR{T} in the listed types
replaced by the corresponding static arguments.
\revision{revival-comprises}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said here,
in a draft note, that the traits listed in a \KWD{comprises} clause
are exactly the traits that immediately extend \VAR{T}
and that each of them must list \VAR{T} in its \KWD{extends} clause.
The revival states the reading of the team's later Types chapter
(Luchangco, 2012) and of the type group's calculus Welterweight Fortress (2012):
the clause says to which types the values of \VAR{T} belong.
A parameterized trait with a static parameter that \VAR{T} does not have
can be listed only at particular static arguments;
it may stand unlisted between \VAR{T} and the listed types,
adding no value outside them,
when at least one trait or object extends it
and every one that does is a subtype of a listed type.
This also answers the third question of the draft note on trait identifiers above,
whether an instantiation of a parameterized trait may be listed: it may.}
\note{
If the \KWD{comprises} clause of a trait \VAR{T} includes ``\EXP{\ldots}''
(and must therefore be in an API),
then in a component exporting the enclosing API,
other traits may explicitly extend \VAR{T},
but these traits may not be declared or imported by the API
(see \secref{apis}).}


For example, the following trait declaration:
\input{\home/basic/examples/Trait.Decl.tex}
declares a trait \TYP{Catalyst} with
no modifiers,
no static parameters,
and
no \KWD{excludes} clauses,
no \KWD{comprises} clauses,
and no \KWD{where} clauses.
Trait \TYP{Catalyst} extends a trait named \TYP{Object}.
A single method (named \VAR{catalyze}) is declared, which
has a parameter of type
\TYP{Reaction} and the return type \TYP{()}.


The following example trait:

%  mass(): Mass
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait} \TYP{Molecule} \KWD{comprises} \{\,\TYP{OrganicMolecule}, \TYP{InorganicMolecule}\,\}\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{mass}()\COLON \TYP{Mass}\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}

== 079f54ea9
4020: - **An inferred generic refuses a coercion that the method it forwards to accepts, on both paths** (2026-09-26, `reviews/numeric-hierarchy-integration-review/row388-container-probe.md`, programs and captures beside it; Astra's prediction in `reviews/numeric-hierarchy-integration-review.md` § 3; ledger row 388 extended; on the flat library 2026-09-27, `reviews/numerics-plan-fable.md` § 3.1 with `numerics-plan-fable/probes/one-shape/`). With an invariant `Box[\T\]`, `b: Box[\Wide\]` and `n: Narrow`, where `Wide` declares `coerce` from `Narrow`: `b.accept(n)` and `acceptBox[\Wide\](b, n)` convert on both paths. The inferred `acceptBox(b, n)` is refused: walk infers `T` as `Object`, then reports a unification error, and the compiled checker says "not applicable". The top-level operator `b n` is refused on both. An operator declared inside `Box` converts compiled and is refused under walk. `RR32` into `Box[\RR64\]` compiled splits as `Wide`/`Narrow` does, and on the flat library so does a `ZZ32` into `Box[\RR64\]` under walk: `scale(b, z)` for `scale[\T\](b: Box[\T\], x: T)` instantiates `T` at `Number` and fails, "Unification error: … (b:Box[\Number\]) got arg Box[\RR64\]" (`one-shape/walk/ScaleZ.walk.txt`, `Scale3.walk.txt`), while `b.accept(z)` converts under walk; on the nested tower walk accepted it by subtyping and returned the integer 3, and the compiled path with its own prelude, which has no `ZZ32`-to-`RR64` coercion, refuses all four forms. So the library's top-level `Vector`- and `Matrix`-scalar operators (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2386-2396`, `:2763-2773`) refuse a narrower scalar that `scale` accepts ("The one library's number tower is flat" under Landed semantics), unless row 388 is fixed or the operators are declared inside the traits; a numeral reaches the same refusal ("Static arguments are inferred from the arguments alone, on both paths, and never through a coercion" below).

# The C series and the APL side quest: state and what comes next

## Where the work stands

The goal is to finish what the designers intended, judged by the latest committed specification (`Specification/`, the July 2012 draft), not to redesign the language, with one program as the measuring stick: microGPT, compiled to bytecode and running fast (the root `CLAUDE.md` § Project goal; `coordinator/POSITIONS.md`, 2026-09-16).

The live thread is the one library. The interpreter's library (`FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`) is to become the library the compiler checks, and the work is to bring the compiled checker to accept it (`coordinator/POSITIONS.md`, 2026-09-21). 156: Each of \KWD{extends}, \KWD{excludes}, and \KWD{comprises} clauses consists
157: of \KWD{extends}, \KWD{excludes}, and \KWD{comprises}
158: respectively followed by a set of trait references
159: separated by commas and enclosed in braces `\txt{\{}' and `\txt{\}}'.
160: If such a clause contains only one trait, the enclosing braces may be elided.
161: In an API (but not a component),
162: a \KWD{comprises} clause may include ``\EXP{\ldots}''.
163: A trait reference listed in the \KWD{comprises} clause is a declared
164: trait identifier (within the same component or an API imported by the
165: component).
166: \note{
167: Victor: Why is this property stated only for a comprises clause?
168: Doesn't it apply to extends and excludes clauses as well?
169: Also, do we really mean ``trait identifier'' above?  Where is that
170: term defined?  Does it include instantiations of parametric traits?}
171: 
172: A trait with an \KWD{extends} clause
233: in the declaration of \VAR{U}.
234: 
235: If a trait declaration of \VAR{T} includes a \KWD{comprises} clause
236: then every type listed in its \KWD{comprises} clause extends \VAR{T},
237: and every value of type \VAR{T} is a value of one of the listed types.
238: A listed type may be an instantiation of a parameterized trait,
239: provided that every static variable that occurs in its static arguments
240: is a static parameter of \VAR{T}.
241: A trait or object that explicitly extends \VAR{T}
242: must be a subtype of a listed type,
243: unless it is a trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause of its own
244: each of whose listed types meets this requirement,
245: or a trait with static parameters
246: such that at least one trait or object extends it
247: and every trait or object that extends it
248: is a subtype of a listed type.
249: If \VAR{T} has static parameters,
250: these statements hold of each instantiation of \VAR{T},
251: with the static parameters of \VAR{T} in the listed types
252: replaced by the corresponding static arguments.
253: \revision{revival-comprises}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said here,
254: in a draft note, that the traits listed in a \KWD{comprises} clause
255: are exactly the traits that immediately extend \VAR{T}
256: and that each of them must list \VAR{T} in its \KWD{extends} clause.
257: The revival states the reading of the team's later Types chapter
258: (Luchangco, 2012) and of the type group's calculus Welterweight Fortress (2012):
259: the clause says to which types the values of \VAR{T} belong.
260: A parameterized trait with a static parameter that \VAR{T} does not have
261: can be listed only at particular static arguments;
262: it may stand unlisted between \VAR{T} and the listed types,
263: adding no value outside them,
264: when at least one trait or object extends it
265: and every one that does is a subtype of a listed type.
266: This also answers the third question of the draft note on trait identifiers above,
267: whether an instantiation of a parameterized trait may be listed: it may.}
268: \note{
269: If the \KWD{comprises} clause of a trait \VAR{T} includes ``\EXP{\ldots}''
270: (and must therefore be in an API),
271: then in a component exporting the enclosing API,
272: other traits may explicitly extend \VAR{T},
273: but these traits may not be declared or imported by the API
274: (see \secref{apis}).}
275: 
276: 
277: For example, the following trait declaration:
278: \input{\home/basic/examples/Trait.Decl.tex}
279: declares a trait \TYP{Catalyst} with
280: no modifiers,
281: no static parameters,
282: and
283: no \KWD{excludes} clauses,
284: no \KWD{comprises} clauses,
285: and no \KWD{where} clauses.
286: Trait \TYP{Catalyst} extends a trait named \TYP{Object}.
287: A single method (named \VAR{catalyze}) is declared, which
288: has a parameter of type
289: \TYP{Reaction} and the return type \TYP{()}.
290: 
291: 
292: The following example trait:
293: %trait Molecule comprises { OrganicMolecule, InorganicMolecule }
294: %  mass(): Mass
295: %end
296: \begin{Fortress}
297: \(\KWD{trait} \TYP{Molecule} \KWD{comprises} \{\,\TYP{OrganicMolecule}, \TYP{InorganicMolecule}\,\}\)\\
298: {\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{mass}()\COLON \TYP{Mass}\)\-\\\poptabs
299: \(\KWD{end}\)
300: \end{Fortress}
301: comprises of two traits: \TYP{OrganicMolecule} and \TYP{InorganicMolecule}.
302: Therefore, the following trait declaration is not allowed:
303: %(* Not allowed! *)
304: %trait ExclusiveMolecule extends Molecule end
305: \begin{Fortress}
306: \(\mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  Not allowed! \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
307: \(\KWD{trait} \TYP{ExclusiveMolecule} \KWD{extends} \TYP{Molecule} \KWD{end}\)
308: \end{Fortress}
309: Traits \TYP{OrganicMolecule} and \TYP{InorganicMolecule} may be exclusive:
310: %trait OrganicMolecule extends Molecule excludes InorganicMolecule end
311: %
312: %trait InorganicMolecule extends Molecule end
313: \begin{Fortress}
314: \(\KWD{trait} \TYP{OrganicMolecule} \KWD{extends} \TYP{Molecule} \KWD{excludes} \TYP{InorganicMolecule} \KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
315: \(\KWD{trait} \TYP{InorganicMolecule} \KWD{extends} \TYP{Molecule} \KWD{end}\)
316: \end{Fortress}
317: \TYP{OrganicMolecule} and \TYP{InorganicMolecule} exclude each other, even
318: though only \TYP{OrganicMolecule} has an \KWD{excludes} clause.
319: For example, the following trait declaration is not allowed:
320: %(* Not allowed! *)
321: %trait InclusiveMolecule extends { InorganicMolecule, OrganicMolecule } end
322: \begin{Fortress}
323: \(\mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  Not allowed! \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
324: \(\KWD{trait} \TYP{InclusiveMolecule} \KWD{extends} \{\,\TYP{InorganicMolecule}, \TYP{OrganicMolecule}\,\} \KWD{end}\)
325: \end{Fortress}
326: 
327: For the same reason, a trait or object may not extend
328: two instantiations of one parameterized trait
329: that exclude each other by instantiation exclusion (\secref{trait-types}),
330: directly or through its supertraits:
331: any two instantiations of one parameterized trait that it extends
332: must have the same static arguments, operator arguments excepted.
333: For example, the following object declaration is not allowed:
334: %trait Parent[\T\] end
335: %(* Not allowed! *)
336: %object Child extends { Parent[\ZZ32\], Parent[\String\] } end
337: \begin{Fortress}
338: \(\KWD{trait}\:\TYP{Parent}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket \KWD{end}\)\\
339: \(\mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  Not allowed! \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
340: \(\KWD{object}\:\TYP{Child} \KWD{extends} \{\,\TYP{Parent}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}32\rrbracket, \TYP{Parent}\llbracket\TYP{String}\rrbracket\,\} \KWD{end}\)

1245: 
1246: \subsection{The traits that extend a closed trait}
1247: \seclabel{revival-comprises}
1248: 
1249: \begin{description}
1250: \item[Affected sections] \secref{trait-decls}.
1251: \item[Change] The first sentence of a draft note in \secref{trait-decls},
1252: which said that the traits listed in a \KWD{comprises} clause are exactly
1253: the traits that immediately extend the declared trait and that they must
1254: explicitly extend it, is replaced by normative text: every listed type
1255: extends the declared trait \VAR{T}, and every value of type \VAR{T} is a
1256: value of one of the listed types; a listed type may be an instantiation of
1257: a parameterized trait whose static arguments contain no static variable
1258: other than the static parameters of \VAR{T}; and a trait or object that explicitly extends
1259: \VAR{T} is a subtype of a listed type, or a trait with a \KWD{comprises}
1260: clause of its own each of whose listed types meets the same requirement, or
1261: a trait with static parameters that at least one trait or object extends
1262: and every trait or object extending it is a subtype of a listed type.
1263: The note's second sentence, on a clause that includes ``\EXP{\ldots}'', is
1264: kept in its note, and the example of \TYP{Molecule} is unchanged.
1265: The new text answers the third question of Victor Luchangco's draft note
1266: on trait identifiers earlier in the section, whether an instantiation of a
1267: parameterized trait may be listed: it may.
1268: \item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival
1269: decided it on 28~September 2026.
1270: The team's later Types chapter (Luchangco, 2012) reads a \KWD{comprises}
1271: clause as coverage: the clause ``specifies a set of types and generic types
1272: determined by the generic type of the declaration'', and an instantiation of
1273: the declared generic type ``is covered by the union of the types in this set
1274: and the corresponding instantiations of the generic type in this set'', one
1275: generic type $G$ determining another $G'$ ``if every parameter of $G'$ is a
1276: parameter of $G$''
1277: (\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick}, lines
1278: 277--283 and 384--390, in the revival's repository).
1279: Welterweight Fortress, the calculus of the type group's paper of 2012
1280: (Chase, Hilburn, Luchangco, Naden, Ryu, Steele, and Tristan, ``Dynamic
1281: Dispatch and Type Inference Semipredicates''), reads it at the level of
1282: values: ``no value can belong to the trait unless it also belongs to one of
1283: the comprised types''; its rule for a trait declaration asks nothing of the
1284: traits that extend a trait with such a clause
1285: (\nolinkurl{Papers/Welterweight/grammar.tick}, lines 21--22;
1286: \nolinkurl{Papers/Welterweight/fig-wellformeddecls.tick}, lines 38--62).
1287: The draft note restated the rule of the compiled type checker of 2009,
1288: under which \library\ could not close their marker of the integer types as
1289: the team meant to: \TYP{AnyIntegral} lists the five integer types, and the
1290: parameterized trait \EXP{\TYP{Integral}\llbracket{}I\rrbracket}, which each
1291: of them extends at itself, stands between them unlisted, as the team's
1292: comment on the declaration records (``not yet: comprises
1293: \EXP{\TYP{Integral}\llbracket{}I\rrbracket} where
1294: \EXP{\llbracket{}I\rrbracket}'', \nolinkurl{Library/FortressLibrary.fsi},
1295: line 434).
1296: \TYP{Integral} has a static parameter that \TYP{AnyIntegral} does not have,
1297: so it can be listed only at particular static arguments, and every value of it is a value of one of the five.
1298: The full reasoning is in
1299: \nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-comprises/decision-record.md}
1300: in the revival's repository.
1301: \item[Effect] The compiled type checker accepts the declaration of
1302: \TYP{AnyIntegral} in \library\ as written
1303: (\nolinkurl{Library/FortressLibrary.fsi}, lines 433--436).
1304: No example of this specification changes: \TYP{ExclusiveMolecule}, which
1305: has no static parameters, is still not allowed.
1306: The compiled type checker enforces the requirement on a trait with static
1307: parameters over the declarations it sees: a trait or object declared in
1308: another component, below such a trait and a subtype of no listed type, is
1309: not refused (row~487 of the revival's gap ledger). It compares the declarations it sees by their names: for a parameterized \VAR{T} its verdict can depend on how an extender spells its static parameters, and a trait of the same simple name in another API counts as an extender (rows~489 and~490).
1310: The interpreter does not check \KWD{comprises} clauses.
1311: The passages that read a \KWD{comprises} clause at the level of types, the
1312: intersection of two traits with such clauses (\secref{internal-types},
1313: \secref{more-specific-rule}) and the definitions an abstract function
1314: declaration requires (\secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations}), are not
1315: revised; whether they are to be restated at the level of values is not
1316: settled.
1317: \item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/traits.tex},
1318: lines 230--241, a draft note:
1319: \begin{quote}
1320: If a trait declaration of \VAR{T} includes a \KWD{comprises} clause
1321: then the traits listed in its \KWD{comprises} clause
1322: are exactly the traits that immediately extend \VAR{T}
1323: and they must explicitly extend \VAR{T}
1324: (i.e., list \VAR{T} in their \KWD{extends} clause).
1325: If the \KWD{comprises} clause of a trait \VAR{T} includes ``\EXP{\ldots}''
1326: (and must therefore be in an API),
1327: then in a component exporting the enclosing API,
1328: other traits may explicitly extend \VAR{T},
1329: but these traits may not be declared or imported by the API
1330: (see \secref{apis}).
1331: \end{quote}
1332: Its second sentence is kept, in its note.
1333: \item[Route C] The same under route~C, under which the self-typed traits
1334: carry \KWD{comprises} clauses of their own (\secref{revival-routec}): a
1335: parameterized trait between a closed trait and its listed types then meets
1336: the requirement through its own clause, and the last case of the
1337: requirement is not needed.
1338: \end{description}
1339: 
1340: \subsection{Passages not yet revised}
1341: \seclabel{revival-notrevised}
1342: 
1343: No passage that instantiation exclusion or the reorganized numeric types
1344: contradict is known to be unrevised.
1345: The rule by which a generic call over two different integer types
1346: infers the narrowest type that both coerce into is to be written into
1347: \chapref{type-inference} together with its implementation
1348: (\secref{revival-numbers}). The result of an integer raised to a negative power is not yet given (\secref{basic-integers}; \secref{revival-integers}).

#!/bin/bash
# name-collision.sh: the simple-name comparison in everyKnownSubtypeListed. SkNameA declares a generic G[\X\] extends
# SkNameD.Closed that nothing extends (zElig's shape) and imports SkNameB, which declares an unrelated G[\X\] and

D=$FORTRESS_HOME/explorations/compile-ladder/rung-comprises-checker/probes/skeptic
CP=$($FORTRESS_HOME/bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
cd $D
for v in base landed; do
  for p in SkNameD SkNameB SkNameA SkNameAlone; do find $FORTRESS_HOME/default_repository/caches -name "*$p*" -exec rm -rf {} + 2>/dev/null; done
  if [ $v = landed ]; then PRE=""; else PRE="$SK/base/cls:"; fi

  done
done

#!/bin/bash
# Compile-path ladder, restricted to the files this rung can affect.
#
# A copy of ../run-ladder.sh with two changes: the ladder root and output
# directory are private to this worktree, and the two whole-corpus loops are
# replaced by one driven by subset.txt (corpus<TAB>file per line).
#
# Pushes every interpreter test program (ProjectFortress/tests/*.fss) and every
# file in ProjectFortress/not_working_library_tests/ through the compiler path
# unchanged and records how far each one gets.
#
# Reproduce:  bash explorations/compile-ladder/run-ladder.sh
# Outputs:    explorations/compile-ladder/raw/<corpus>/<name>.{compile,run}
#             explorations/compile-ladder/results.tsv
#
# The run uses a private cache tree so it never touches default_repository/caches
# (fortress.caches system property + FORTRESS_CACHES env; ProjectProperties.java:283,
# same mechanism the suite uses at build.xml:941-943), and a private java.io.tmpdir
# so the 5.8 MB Rats! temp directory of every grammar-importing run (RatsUtil.java:138-144)
# is swept per file instead of filling the disk.

set -u

# env.sh's exports without its rm of /tmp/fortress*rats, which the other rung's runs may be using
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH="/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH" FORTRESS_THREADS=1
export FORTRESS_HOME="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../../.." && pwd)"
unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS

LADDER_ROOT="${LADDER_ROOT:-$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp/ladder-r1}"
export LADDER_CACHES="$LADDER_ROOT/ladder-caches"

## 9. The ladder subset

The one file whose recorded first error in `explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/raw/` names this refusal is `tests/atomicList.fss`, for the non-generic `object ListError extends Exception` against the compiler library's `Exception comprises { UncheckedException, CheckedException }`. It was run before and after with the restricted driver, copied as `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-comprises-checker/run-subset.sh` and `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-comprises-checker/subset.txt` with a private `LADDER_ROOT` and without `env.sh`'s `rm` of `/tmp/fortress*rats`.
- Its compile output is byte-identical: three errors, rc 255 (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-comprises-checker/ladder-pre/results.tsv`, `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-comprises-checker/ladder-post/results.tsv` and their `raw/`).
- None of the ladder's 85 files (`explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-7R/gate/ladder/ladder.tsv`) contains `comprises` (grep). A ladder file can therefore move only through the compiler library's clauses, which compiled before the edit and cannot lose an acceptance.

## 10. The name grep (step 7)

Every name the two tests and the edit add was grepped in `ProjectFortress/tests/`, every `*_tests/` directory, `test_library/`, `LibraryBuiltin/`, `Library/` and the whole of `src/com/sun/fortress/` (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-comprises-checker/probes/names-grep.txt`). No competing declaration was found. `Closed` occurs in a string and a comment. `Tagged` is a `private object` of the `QuickCheck` component (`Library/QuickCheck.fss:937`), which no compiler test imports.

## 11. Every measured defect and its home

- **Row 459, the clause refused: repaired, home 1.** The assertions are `ComprisesGenericSubtrait.fss`'s three, which pass (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-comprises-checker/probes/post-edit-tests.txt`), and the link that precedes them. The row closes.

> The traits that extend a closed trait
> Affected sections Section 10.1.
> Change The first sentence of a draft note in Section 10.1, which said that the traits listed in a comprises clause are
> exactly the traits that immediately extend the declared trait and that they must explicitly extend it, is replaced
> by normative text: every listed type extends the declared trait T , and every value of type T is a value of one
> of the listed types; a listed type may be an instantiation of a parameterized trait whose static arguments contain
> no static variable other than the static parameters of T ; and a trait or object that explicitly extends T is a
> subtype of a listed type, or a trait with a comprises clause of its own each of whose listed types meets the
> same requirement, or a trait with static parameters that at least one trait or object extends and every trait or
> object extending it is a subtype of a listed type. The note’s second sentence, on a clause that includes “. . . ”, is
> kept in its note, and the example of Molecule is unchanged. The new text answers the third question of Victor
> Luchangco’s draft note on trait identifiers earlier in the section, whether an instantiation of a parameterized trait
> may be listed: it may.
> Rationale This change does not follow from route A; the revival decided it on 28 September 2026. The team’s
> later Types chapter (Luchangco, 2012) reads a comprises clause as coverage: the clause “specifies a set of
> types and generic types determined by the generic type of the declaration”, and an instantiation of the declared generic type “is covered by the union of the types in this set and the corresponding instantiations of
> the generic type in this set”, one generic type G determining another G′ “if every parameter of G′ is a parameter of G” (Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick, lines 277–283
> and 384–390, in the revival’s repository). Welterweight Fortress, the calculus of the type group’s paper of
> 2012 (Chase, Hilburn, Luchangco, Naden, Ryu, Steele, and Tristan, “Dynamic Dispatch and Type Inference
> Semipredicates”), reads it at the level of values: “no value can belong to the trait unless it also belongs
> to one of the comprised types”; its rule for a trait declaration asks nothing of the traits that extend a trait
> with such a clause (Papers/Welterweight/grammar.tick, lines 21–22; Papers/Welterweight/
> fig-wellformeddecls.tick, lines 38–62). The draft note restated the rule of the compiled type checker
> of 2009, under which the Fortress standard libraries could not close their marker of the integer types as the
> team meant to: AnyIntegral lists the five integer types, and the parameterized trait IntegralJIK , which each
> of them extends at itself, stands between them unlisted, as the team’s comment on the declaration records (“not
> yet: comprises IntegralJIK where JIK ”, Library/FortressLibrary.fsi, line 434). Integral has a
> static parameter that AnyIntegral does not have, so it can be listed only at particular static arguments, and
> every value of it is a value of one of the five. The full reasoning is in explorations/compile-ladder/
> rung-spec-comprises/decision-record.md in the revival’s repository.
> Effect The compiled type checker accepts the declaration of AnyIntegral in the Fortress standard libraries as
> written (Library/FortressLibrary.fsi, lines 433–436). No example of this specification changes:
> ExclusiveMolecule, which has no static parameters, is still not allowed. The compiled type checker enforces

def flush():
